screens.title: Stub vs Mock — A Practical Distinction
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition. A stub is a test double that supplies predetermined data so the system under test receives controlled inputs. A mock does more: it records calls and arguments so the test can later assert what the system did to the dependency. For example, if you need a dependency to return specific user data so your function can proceed, a stub is ideal. But when you need to ensure an email was sent to the right recipient, a mock is appropriate because you care about the interaction itself. A common misconception is that mocks are just fancier stubs; they are not. The difference is usage: stubs control flows, mocks verify behavior. Another misconception is that every external call must be mocked — instead, mock only those collaborators that produce important side effects or define a boundary of responsibility. In practice, prefer stubs when the dependency only supplies data and prefer mocks when you must assert that a side-effectful method was called. As a closing question: when you read a failing test that asserts a call on an internal helper, ask whether that assertion verifies public behavior or internal choreography. If the latter, consider replacing the verification with a public-facing assertion.

Core Concept
Stub vs Mock — A Practical Distinction
When to supply data and when to record interactions
Stub (control inputs)
  • Supplies fixed return values so the unit can proceed.
  • Used when you only care about inputs, not calls.
  • Example: stubbed repository returning a user record.
Mnemonic: feed data into the system
Mock (verify behavior)
  • Records method calls, arguments, and counts for assertions.
  • Used when side effects (email, logging) must be verified.
  • Example: mock email service to assert a welcome email was attempted.
Mnemonic: a witness logs what happened
Misconception
Mocks are not only fancier stubs; they are used to verify interactions, not just supply values.
Pro tip
Mock direct collaborators that represent meaningful side effects; avoid mocking internal pure helpers.
Key takeaway
Choose the double that matches what you care about: data or interactions.

Code Walkthrough
UserService — Verifying Email Sending
A focused test that checks interaction with EmailService
Starter test (visual)
import unittest
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
from user_service import UserService, UserRepository, EmailService

class TestUserService(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.mock_user_repo = MagicMock(spec=UserRepository)
        self.mock_email_service = MagicMock(spec=EmailService)
        self.user_service = UserService(self.mock_user_repo, self.mock_email_service)

    def test_register_user_sends_welcome_email(self):
        username = "johndoe"
        email = "john.doe@example.com"

        self.user_service.register_user(username, email)

        self.mock_email_service.send_welcome_email.assert_called_once_with(email, username)
Explanation
  • MagicMock with spec ensures the mock only has the real API surface.
  • assert_called_once_with checks both the single call and its arguments.
  • Do not perform real side effects during unit tests.
Concrete scenario
When a new user registers, the system must attempt to send a welcome email. This test confirms that attempt without sending real mail.
Key Takeaway

Assert interactions that represent meaningful side effects and configure mock return values when the unit depends on them.

screens.title: Common MagicMock Assertions
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson reviews the common assertion methods available on MagicMock objects and when to use each. assert_called_once_with verifies that a method was called exactly once with the expected arguments; use it when a single call is required by the behavior. assert_called_with checks that the latest call matched the arguments, useful when multiple calls are acceptable but you need to confirm a particular invocation. assert_any_call confirms that at least one call in the history matched the arguments, which is useful for unordered or repeated interactions. assert_not_called ensures a collaborator was never invoked — handy for validating that side effects are skipped when input validation fails. A frequent mistake is using assert_called_with when you meant assert_called_once_with; the first does not fail if there were multiple calls. Another error is failing to set return_value on a mock when the system under test consumes the return. In practice, pick the assertion that captures the contract you expect: exact call count for strict behavior, any-call for flexible sequences, and not-called for negative flows. To reinforce learning, try writing three small tests: one each for exact call, any-call, and not-called.

Process Flow
Common MagicMock Assertions
Pick the assertion that matches the behavioral contract
assert_called_once_with()
Use when exactly one call is required with specific args.
assert_called_with()
Verifies the most recent call's args; doesn't enforce count.
assert_any_call()
Checks that at least one call matched the provided args.
assert_not_called()
Asserts the mock was never invoked; use for negative paths.
Common mistake
Using assert_called_with when multiple calls are possible will not catch extra unwanted calls.
Pro tip
Combine call assertions with checks on return_value when the SUT consumes a mock's return.

screens.title: When to Mock — Practical Guidelines
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding whether to mock a collaborator is as much a design choice as a testing technique. Mock when the collaborator performs an external side effect or defines a boundary you want to isolate: sending email, writing an audit log, or publishing messages. Do not mock internal pure functions whose result you could verify by checking the unit's return value or state change. Over-mocking happens when you assert many small interactions that reflect internal choreography rather than public behavior. This makes tests brittle: small refactors break tests even though the public contract remains. A practical guideline is to mock collaborators that are slow, flaky, or outside test control, and to assert outcomes that represent the unit's contract. When in doubt, prefer a simpler assertion that captures what the consumer of your unit would rely on. For example, verify that a repository persisted a user by checking the returned user id or public state rather than asserting every helper call in the save path. Ask: does the assertion protect an external contract or internal implementation? In practical terms, choosing mocks without over-coupling tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
When to Mock — Practical Guidelines
Balance isolation with test resilience
Mock these
  • External systems: email, queues, external APIs
  • Slow or flaky dependencies
  • Collaborators that represent a behavior boundary
Avoid mocking these
  • Internal pure helpers whose results can be asserted
  • Many small internal calls that reflect implementation details
  • Anything that makes tests fragile to refactor
Check your understanding
If a test breaks after refactoring private helper calls but the behavior is unchanged, did you over-mock? Consider changing assertions to public outcomes.

screens.title: Over-mocking — Why Tests Become Brittle
screens.narratorSegment: Over-mocking is the anti-pattern of mocking too many collaborators or asserting too many internal calls. Tests become brittle because they tie the test suite to the current implementation instead of the unit's external contract. A typical scenario: you refactor an internal helper into two steps and suddenly many tests that asserted those helper calls fail, even though the public behavior is unchanged. To prevent this, verify outward-facing effects and important side-effect calls only. If you must assert several interactions, consider whether the unit under test has grown too complex and might benefit from clearer boundaries or additional responsibility extraction. Another practical technique is to use higher-level assertions — for example, verify that an email-sending method was called rather than asserting the sequence of internal formatting methods. A misconception is that more assertions equal better tests; in fact, each extra assertion on internals increases maintenance cost. End with this reflective question: does each assertion protect a meaningful behavior the consumer relies on? In practical terms, recognize and prevent fragile tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture
Spec and return values
Make mocks realistic and prevent accidental API misuse
# Use spec to mirror real API surface
self.mock_user_repo = MagicMock(spec=UserRepository)

# If save_user returns created user, configure it
self.mock_user_repo.save_user.return_value = {"id": 123, "username": "johndoe", "email": "john.doe@example.com"}
Why this matters
Spec helps tests fail early on API mismatches. Return values ensure the SUT receives expected data shapes, preventing obscure errors.
Misconception
Spec is not a substitute for validating return contents; design return_value deliberately for the test's needs.
Key Takeaway

Combine spec and return_value to make mocks predictable and closer to production behavior where the SUT relies on returned data.

screens.title: Forgetting to Configure Return Values
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent source of confusing failures is when a mock is used in place of a collaborator that normally returns data used by the system under test, but the test never sets return_value. The SUT then reads the mock object instead of the expected structure, causing attribute errors or logic branches to behave unexpectedly. For example, if save_user should return a dict with id, username, and email but the mock returns a MagicMock by default, code that accesses user_data['id'] will fail. The remedy is straightforward: when the SUT depends on the collaborator's return, set mock. method. return_value to a minimal representative object. Another option is to design the SUT to be resilient by validating returns, but in tests it's generally simpler and clearer to set the mock return. A misconception is that mocks always behave like stubs — remember they record calls by default but return another mock unless configured. Conclude by asking: does your test assume a particular return shape? If so, make it explicit in the mock setup. screens.title: Edge Cases: Exceptions and Side Effects on Mocks
screens.narratorSegment: Mocks can also simulate exceptions and side effects to test error handling. You can set side_effect on a MagicMock method to raise an exception or to execute a callable that returns specific values per call. Use this to ensure your code handles downstream failures correctly. For example, if save_user might raise a database error, set mock_user_repo. save_user. side_effect = Exception('db error') and assert that UserService responds by not calling the email sender and by propagating or handling the error as intended. A common misconception is to assert both the exception and several internal calls — instead, assert the critical public behavior such as no email sent and an appropriate error response or propagation. Also be careful to reset side_effect between tests or create fresh mocks per test to avoid cross-test interference. screens.title: Putting It Together — Test Design Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Before you finalize an interaction test, run through a short checklist. First, identify the behavior you want to protect — a public side effect or contract. Second, decide whether a mock is required: mock only collaborators that perform significant side effects or are outside test control. Third, create the mock with spec to prevent A P I drift and set return_value when the SUT consumes results. Fourth, choose the correct assertion: assert_called_once_with for exact single-call expectations, assert_any_call for flexible matches, and assert_not_called for negative paths. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on mocks — test doubles that let you verify behavior. Unlike stubs that simply supply data, mocks record interactions so you can assert that specific methods were called, how many times, and with what arguments. This matters whenever side effects are important: sending an email, logging an audit entry, publishing a message, or updating an external system. You will see concrete examples using Python's unittest. mock and a small UserService that triggers an EmailService. We'll practice assert_called_once_with, assert_not_called, and when to set return values on mocks. We'll also explore the pitfall of over-mocking: verifying internal implementation details makes tests brittle and slows refactoring. By the end of this chapter you'll know how to choose where a mock belongs, write clear interaction assertions that verify behavior without coupling tests to internals, and work through a hands-on activity that checks audit logging in a transaction processor. Consider the mock as a witness — you ask it what your code did. Your task is to verify the observable actions that matter to the unit's contract, not every internal step. Ready to learn how to record and check those interactions confidently?

These objectives map directly to practical skills in writing unit tests that verify behavior. First, you will be able to explain the difference between a stub and a mock: a stub supplies controlled data while a mock records calls so you can assert interactions. Second, you will implement mocks with a testing framework and use assertion helpers to inspect call history. Third, you will write tests that assert method calls and arguments for real examples like sending emails or logging an audit entry. Fourth, you will learn to identify when mocks are the right choice and avoid over-mocking to keep tests resilient. Each objective pairs a compact skill statement with why it matters in practice. For example, verifying that an email-sending call happened prevents regressions in notification flows without the flakiness of sending real email during test runs. Throughout the chapter we show concrete patterns, starter tests, and a hands-on activity so you can practice these objectives. By the end you will not only know the A P I methods to use, but also how to decide what to verify and how to keep tests maintainable. Ask yourself as you learn: does this assertion check public behavior or private implementation?

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and assessment. You'll implement unit tests for examples like UserService and TransactionProcessor, using MagicMock to verify critical side effects such as sending emails or logging audit entries. Each objective includes a competency milestone: set up a mock with a spec, configure return values when the system under test depends on them, and choose the correct assertion for a behavior. In practice you will run tests that assert a mock method was called once with expected arguments, and tests that confirm a method was not called when validation fails. For assessment, you will answer conceptual questions about which assertion matches a verification need and explain the risk of over-mocking. The hands-on activity returns a starter test file where you replace placeholders with concrete assertions, giving you focused practice. As you work, keep a habit of asking whether you are verifying the unit's public contract or its private choreography. That question will guide whether a mock is appropriate and whether your assertions should be narrow or resilient to implementation changes.

Start with a clear definition. A stub is a test double that supplies predetermined data so the system under test receives controlled inputs. A mock does more: it records calls and arguments so the test can later assert what the system did to the dependency. For example, if you need a dependency to return specific user data so your function can proceed, a stub is ideal. But when you need to ensure an email was sent to the right recipient, a mock is appropriate because you care about the interaction itself. A common misconception is that mocks are just fancier stubs; they are not. The difference is usage: stubs control flows, mocks verify behavior. Another misconception is that every external call must be mocked — instead, mock only those collaborators that produce important side effects or define a boundary of responsibility. In practice, prefer stubs when the dependency only supplies data and prefer mocks when you must assert that a side-effectful method was called. As a closing question: when you read a failing test that asserts a call on an internal helper, ask whether that assertion verifies public behavior or internal choreography. If the latter, consider replacing the verification with a public-facing assertion.

We'll walk through the UserService example where registering a user both saves user data and triggers a welcome email. The goal of the test is not to send a real email but to assert that the email service's method was called with the expected email and username. In tests you set up MagicMock objects for UserRepository and EmailService, often using the spec argument so attribute errors surface when the implementation diverges. After calling register_user with valid inputs, you assert that send_welcome_email was called exactly once with the right arguments. A common pitfall is assuming the mock returns realistic data — if UserService depends on a returned object from save_user, configure mock_user_repo. save_user. return_value appropriately. Also watch out for argument order: the test must match the method signature used by the implementation. As an example, the assertion assert_called_once_with(email, username) checks both the exact arguments and the call count. A closing thought: if your test must assert many internal helper calls to pass, you may be over-mocking — prefer verifying the outward side effect where possible. In practical terms, test that register_user triggers a welcome email. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This lesson reviews the common assertion methods available on MagicMock objects and when to use each. assert_called_once_with verifies that a method was called exactly once with the expected arguments; use it when a single call is required by the behavior. assert_called_with checks that the latest call matched the arguments, useful when multiple calls are acceptable but you need to confirm a particular invocation. assert_any_call confirms that at least one call in the history matched the arguments, which is useful for unordered or repeated interactions. assert_not_called ensures a collaborator was never invoked — handy for validating that side effects are skipped when input validation fails. A frequent mistake is using assert_called_with when you meant assert_called_once_with; the first does not fail if there were multiple calls. Another error is failing to set return_value on a mock when the system under test consumes the return. In practice, pick the assertion that captures the contract you expect: exact call count for strict behavior, any-call for flexible sequences, and not-called for negative flows. To reinforce learning, try writing three small tests: one each for exact call, any-call, and not-called.

Deciding whether to mock a collaborator is as much a design choice as a testing technique. Mock when the collaborator performs an external side effect or defines a boundary you want to isolate: sending email, writing an audit log, or publishing messages. Do not mock internal pure functions whose result you could verify by checking the unit's return value or state change. Over-mocking happens when you assert many small interactions that reflect internal choreography rather than public behavior. This makes tests brittle: small refactors break tests even though the public contract remains. A practical guideline is to mock collaborators that are slow, flaky, or outside test control, and to assert outcomes that represent the unit's contract. When in doubt, prefer a simpler assertion that captures what the consumer of your unit would rely on. For example, verify that a repository persisted a user by checking the returned user id or public state rather than asserting every helper call in the save path. Tests become brittle because they tie the test suite to the current implementation instead of the unit's external contract. To prevent this, verify outward-facing effects and important side-effect calls only. If you must assert several interactions, consider whether the unit under test has grown too complex and might benefit from clearer boundaries or additional responsibility extraction. A misconception is that more assertions equal better tests; in fact, each extra assertion on internals increases maintenance cost. Before you finalize an interaction test, run through a short checklist. First, identify the behavior you want to protect — a public side effect or contract. Second, decide whether a mock is required: mock only collaborators that perform significant side effects or are outside test control. Third, create the mock with spec to prevent A P I drift and set return_value when the SUT consumes results. Fourth, choose the correct assertion: assert_called_once_with for exact single-call expectations, assert_any_call for flexible matches, and assert_not_called for negative paths. Fifth, consider failure modes and use side_effect to simulate exceptions. Sixth, avoid asserting internal helper calls that reflect implementation details. This checklist keeps tests focused, readable, and maintainable. Second, choose your test doubles carefully: stubs for controlling inputs, mocks for verifying side effects. Third, avoid over-mocking; verify public behavior and meaningful side effects rather than internals so your tests remain resilient to refactors.
